NEW YORK (CNN)  -- Obesity is the No. 1 health crisis in the United States, and the nation could be at risk without immediate action, former President Clinton said at CNN's first Fit Nation Summit. CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta and former President Clinton lead the discussion at the first Fit Nation Summit. "We need to do something about it for our children, and for our country, because something like this could easily collapse our nation if we don't act now," Clinton said. Clinton and CNN's chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, gathered with experts from across the country Wednesday to explore solutions to America's obesity crisis. Two-thirds of adult Americans are overweight or obese; the same is true for one-third of U.S. children, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Obesity carries increased risk of myriad health problems, including hypertension, diabetes, heart disease and arthritis. Gupta, Clinton and a panel of experts addressed such proposed solutions as healthy school lunches, elimination of trans fats, the need for healthier food in urban communities and the importance of supporting community-based efforts to fight obesity.  Watch Gupta explain the solutions proposed at the Fit Nation Summit » . Clinton, who's been tackling the obesity issue over the past few years with his Alliance for a Healthier Generation, stressed the need to help educate people about the importance of a healthy diet and exercising together. Motivating Americans, especially kids, won't be easy, Clinton said. "They need to be handled with care. Kids need to know it's important, but [fitness] can't be boring," he said. "There's no shame, there's no embarrassment. We have to let them know it's all good, but you have to do it." Michael Jacobson, director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest and a strong advocate against trans fats in foods, stressed that the Food and Drug Administration should ban trans fats altogether and stop leaving it up to local and state governments. Trans fats, at one time, thought to be good fat substitutes, over the years have been shown to raise LDL or bad cholesterol in people and lower their HDL, or good cholesterol. "They're just not good for our health, Jacobson said. However, Dr. Robert Eckel, former president of the American Heart Association, warned, "Although we support the removal of trans fats, our biggest concern is what they'll be replaced with. We need to think about that, because there will be a substitute." The panel took questions from an audience of 150 people -- mostly obesity experts or those who work in industries that deal with obesity. Gupta was inspired to launch Fit Nation, an ongoing, multiplatform, grass-roots initiative against obesity. Over the past three years, Gupta and the CNN Medical Unit have crisscrossed the country, asking Americans to take charge of their weight by exercising more and eating healthier. This year, Gupta traveled from Michigan to California asking the public to pledge to add 1 million hours to their collective lives by getting off the couch and exercising. Since he began the tour in April, the campaign has surpassed its goal, with exercise pledges close to four times that amount. Gupta said he hopes that legislators and administrators who can make a difference in policy and perhaps change attitudes about obesity will hear the solutions discussed at the summit. "I''ve covered a lot of stories on obesity," Gupta said. "There's a battle going on, and we need to win the battle. I've talked to people out there and many are just blasé. "This is our opportunity to make them care." E-mail to a friend .

***

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — Describing obesity as the nation’s foremost health crisis, former President Bill Clinton warned at CNN’s inaugural Fit Nation Summit that the United States faces severe risks without immediate, decisive action. 

Co-leading the discussion alongside CNN’s Chief Medical Correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, Clinton emphasized the urgency of the situation: “We need to do something about it for our children and for our country, because something like this could easily collapse our nation if we don’t act now.”

On Wednesday, Clinton and Dr. Gupta convened a panel of national experts to explore actionable solutions to America’s growing obesity epidemic. Data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention underscores the scale of the challenge: two-thirds of American adults and one-third of American children are currently overweight or obese. The condition carries a heightened risk for a myriad of health complications, including hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, and arthritis.

The panel examined several key proposals, including improving the nutritional quality of school lunches, eliminating trans fats, expanding access to healthy food in urban communities, and bolstering support for grassroots, community-based health initiatives. 

Clinton, who has spent recent years tackling the issue through his Alliance for a Healthier Generation, highlighted the necessity of educating the public on the benefits of a healthy diet and shared physical activity. Acknowledging that motivating the public—especially youth—will be challenging, Clinton noted: “They need to be handled with care. Kids need to know it’s important, but fitness cannot be boring. There is no shame, there is no embarrassment. We have to let them know it is all positive, but emphasize that they must take action.”

The summit also addressed regulatory interventions regarding dietary fats. Michael Jacobson, Director of the Center for Science in the Public Interest and a prominent advocate against trans fats, urged the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to institute a nationwide ban rather than leaving policy decisions to state and local governments. Once erroneously believed to be safe substitutes, trans fats have been proven to raise LDL ("bad") cholesterol while lowering HDL ("good") cholesterol. “They are simply not good for our health,” Jacobson stated.

Providing a nuanced perspective, Dr. Robert Eckel, former president of the American Heart Association, cautioned: “Although we support the removal of trans fats, our biggest concern is what they will be replaced with. We need to think about that, because there will be a substitute.”

The panel subsequently took questions from an audience of 150 participants, primarily consisting of healthcare experts and industry professionals specializing in obesity management. 

The summit builds on *Fit Nation*, an ongoing, multiplatform grassroots initiative created by Dr. Gupta to combat obesity. Over the past three years, Dr. Gupta and the CNN Medical Unit have traveled extensively across the country, encouraging Americans to take charge of their health through improved nutrition and regular exercise. 

During a recent tour spanning from Michigan to California, Dr. Gupta challenged the public to pledge a collective 1 million hours of physical activity. Since the campaign launched in April, it has far exceeded its initial target, securing pledges nearly four times its original goal.

Dr. Gupta expressed optimism that lawmakers and administrators in positions to shape policy and influence public perception will adopt the solutions presented at the summit. 

“I have covered a lot of stories on obesity,” Dr. Gupta said. “There is a battle going on, and we need to win it. I’ve talked to people out there, and many are simply blasé. This is our opportunity to make them care.”

**Confronting the Crisis: Leaders and Experts Unveil Strategies at CNN’s Fit Nation Summit to Combat the U.S. Obesity Epidemic**

The United States faces an unprecedented public health crisis as obesity rates continue to rise at an alarming pace. Affecting more than forty percent of American adults and nearly twenty percent of children, the epidemic has expanded far beyond an individual health concern, developing into a critical national issue that threatens to overwhelm healthcare systems and diminish quality of life for future generations. To address the root causes of this growing emergency and forge a path forward, national health experts, policymakers, and advocates gathered at CNN’s *Fit Nation Summit*, hosted by CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta, alongside featured keynote speaker former President Bill Clinton.

The summit served as a crucial platform to examine how the modern American landscape—characterized by sedentary lifestyles, hyper-processed foods, and socioeconomic disparities—has fostered an environment where maintaining a healthy weight is uniquely difficult. Opening the discussion, Dr. Sanjay Gupta emphasized that individual willpower alone cannot overcome a systemic environment designed to promote overconsumption and inactivity. He noted that childhood obesity, in particular, poses a devastating threat, as conditions once reserved for middle-aged adults, such as Type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, and early-stage cardiovascular disease, are now routinely diagnosed in adolescents.

Former President Bill Clinton brought both political weight and personal insight to the conversation. Following his own highly publicized heart surgery and subsequent transition to a plant-based diet, Clinton has made pediatric health a cornerstone of his post-presidential public service through the Clinton Foundation and the Alliance for a Healthier Generation. During the summit, Clinton stressed that changing the nation’s health trajectory requires bold, systemic policy interventions rather than incremental suggestions. He argued that the fight against obesity must be treated with the same urgency as a national security issue, noting that a nation burdened by chronic illness faces severe economic and societal limitations.

A central theme of the summit was the necessity of implementing a multifaceted, multi-layered strategy. Panellists agreed that no single reform could solve the epidemic; instead, meaningful progress demands sweeping changes across schools, industries, and local communities. 

Among the primary solutions championed at the summit was the overhaul of school nutrition programs. Because children spend a significant portion of their daily lives in academic settings, schools represent ground zero in the battle against childhood obesity. Experts called for stricter nutritional standards, the elimination of sugary beverages and high-calorie junk foods from vending machines, and increased funding for fresh, locally sourced fruits, vegetables, and whole grains in cafeteria lunches. 

In addition to dietary improvements in schools, the panel highlighted the impact of regulatory measures, such as municipal bans on artificial trans fats and mandatory calorie labeling on restaurant menus. These public health initiatives, which have already seen success in several major metropolitan areas, empower consumers to make informed choices while incentivizing the food industry to reformulate products to be healthier. 

Physical activity was identified as the second essential pillar of the solution. Experts urged school districts to resist cutting physical education classes and recess—practices that have unfortunately become common under budget constraints and heightened academic testing pressures. Beyond the classroom, community leaders were encouraged to invest in infrastructure that supports active living, such as public parks, safe bike lanes, and walkable neighborhoods, particularly in low-income areas that often lack safe spaces for outdoor recreation.

The summit concluded with a sober reminder of the stakes. Without decisive, coordinated intervention, the current trajectory could lead to catastrophic long-term health consequences, including reduced life expectancy for today's youth and trillions of dollars in preventable medical costs. However, as President Clinton, Dr. Gupta, and participating experts emphasized, the crisis is not insurmountable. By uniting public policy, private sector cooperation, and community-driven fitness initiatives, the nation can transform its health landscape, protect its children, and secure a healthier, more resilient future.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article covering the first Fit Nation Summit hosted by Dr. Sanjay Gupta and former President Bill Clinton. Include quotes on childhood obesity, CDC statistics, and the debate surrounding trans fat bans.
counterfactuals.output:
**NEW YORK (CNN) —** Sounding the alarm on what they termed a national security and public health emergency, former President Bill Clinton and CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta convened the inaugural "Fit Nation Summit" on Tuesday, bringing together policy leaders, medical experts, and advocates to confront America's expanding obesity crisis.

The summit, held in New York City, focused heavily on the alarming rise of childhood obesity, the staggering economic toll on the healthcare system, and the increasingly heated political debates surrounding government intervention in the American diet—including municipal bans on artificial trans fats.

"We are looking at a generation of children who could be the first in American history to live shorter lives than their parents," Clinton told a packed auditorium of healthcare professionals and policymakers. "If we don’t address childhood obesity right now—in our schools, in our communities, and in our homes—the financial and human costs will simply overwhelm us."

### A Childhood Health Emergency

The summit highlighted the stark realities facing American youth. Clinton, whose William J. Clinton Foundation has made childhood health a primary focus, noted that childhood obesity is no longer just a aesthetic or social concern, but a precursor to adult chronic illnesses previously unheard of in young populations.

Dr. Gupta emphasized that pediatricians are now diagnosing children with conditions historically reserved for adults.

"Thirty years ago, type 2 diabetes in kids was practically nonexistent. Today, it accounts for up to half of all newly diagnosed cases of diabetes in children," Gupta said during a keynote panel. "This isn't just about weight; it’s about the fundamental, long-term cardiovascular and metabolic health of our nation's future."

Gupta pointed out that early intervention is critical, calling childhood obesity "a crisis hidden in plain sight."

### The Hard Numbers: CDC Statistics Paint a Grim Picture

Underpinning the summit’s urgent tone were sobering statistics from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 

According to CDC data presented at the conference:
*   Approximately **17% (or 12.5 million)** of children and adolescents aged 2 to 19 are obese—a rate that has nearly tripled in a single generation.
*   More than **one-third of American adults**—over 72 million people—are classified as obese.
*   Obesity-related medical conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer, cost the U.S. healthcare system an estimated **$147 billion annually**.
*   On average, annual medical spending for an obese individual is **$1,429 higher** than for someone of a healthy weight.

CDC representatives at the summit warned that without aggressive intervention, obesity rates could continue to climb, threatening to bankrupt state and federal healthcare budgets.

### The Great Trans Fat Debate: Public Health vs. Personal Choice

While participants agreed on the scale of the crisis, the summit laid bare deep divisions over how far government should go to regulate what Americans eat. Central to the discussion was the mounting debate over trans fat bans.

Artificial trans fats—partially hydrogenated oils widely used in fried foods and baked goods—have been linked by health experts to elevated LDL ("bad") cholesterol and increased risks of coronary heart disease. Cities like New York have moved to ban trans fats in restaurants, a move that panel experts fiercely debated.

Supporters of government bans argued that voluntary measures by the food industry are inadequate.

"Trans fat is a synthetic toxin with zero nutritional value," said one prominent public health panelist. "Removing it from the food supply is no different than removing lead from paint. It is a fundamental obligation of public health policy."

However, critics and representatives from the food and restaurant industries pushed back, raising concerns over government overreach and economic burdens on small businesses.

"Where does the 'nanny state' stop?" argued a representative from a food industry advocacy group. "Today it’s trans fats, tomorrow it’s sugar, and next week it’s portion sizes. Consumers deserve education and choice, not mandates that tell them what they are allowed to put on their dinner plates."

Addressing the controversy, Clinton urged a pragmatic middle ground, emphasizing partnerships with food manufacturers to voluntarily reformulate products, while acknowledging that local governments may feel compelled to act if public health metrics fail to improve.

### The Road Ahead

The Fit Nation Summit concluded with a call to action aimed at schools, local governments, and private industry. Recommendations included restoring mandatory daily physical education in public schools, eliminating sugar-sweetened beverages from vending machines on school grounds, and creating tax incentives for supermarkets to open in underserved urban "food deserts."

For Gupta, the event marked a critical step toward shifting the national conversation from diagnosis to action.

"We cannot cure our way out of this epidemic with prescription drugs or surgeries," Gupta said in his closing remarks. "The cure for obesity begins with prevention, policy, and a cultural shift in how we view food and movement in everyday American life."

**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**

**WASHINGTON** — Former President Bill Clinton and CNN Chief Medical Correspondent Dr. Sanjay Gupta announced a major joint initiative on Tuesday aimed at tackling the growing childhood obesity epidemic in the United States, uniting political clout with medical expertise in a bipartisan, nationwide campaign.

The new partnership, dubbed the **“Healthy Futures Initiative,”** aims to reverse rising obesity rates among American youth over the next decade through school food reform, urban agriculture expansion, and a massive public health awareness campaign.

The announcement was made at the National Press Club, where both leaders warned that childhood obesity poses not only a critical public health emergency, but a threat to the nation’s long-term economic stability and military readiness. 

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), nearly 20% of American children and adolescents—roughly 14.7 million individuals—are classified as obese, a number that rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“We are shortchanging our children before they even get a fair start,” Clinton said during his opening remarks. “When I underwent heart surgery years ago, it was a wake-up call for me personally. But for millions of kids across America, the health crisis isn't waiting until adulthood—it's happening right now in their schools, their neighborhoods, and their homes. We have to change the environment surrounding our kids so that the healthy choice becomes the easy choice.”

Clinton, whose foundation launched the Alliance for a Healthier Generation in 2005, brings decades of policy influence and corporate negotiating power to the table. Dr. Gupta, a practicing neurosurgeon and one of the nation’s most trusted medical broadcasters, brings a focus on evidence-based medicine and public communication.

Gupta emphasized that the initiative will move away from traditional "shaming" tactics and instead focus on structural fixes to what he described as an "obesogenic environment."

“For too long, we’ve treated obesity as a failure of individual willpower, especially when it comes to children,” Gupta said. “The science tells us a completely different story. This is a systemic issue driven by the flood of ultra-processed foods, the disappearance of safe physical spaces for play, and deep-seated health inequities. You can’t tell a child to eat better if their neighborhood doesn't have a grocery store, or to play outside if there are no safe parks.”

### A Three-Pronged Strategy

The Healthy Futures Initiative will focus on three core pillars:

1. **School & Community Food Reform:** Partnering with major food distributors to reduce added sugars and ultra-processed ingredients in public school lunches, while offering grants to install hydroponic farms and fresh salad bars in underserved school districts.
2. **Eliminating Food Deserts:** Working with local governments and private investors to incentivize supermarket chains and mobile farm markets to operate in low-income urban and rural areas.
3. **Digital Health Literacy:** Launching an interactive, youth-focused media campaign led by Gupta to help parents and kids understand nutrition labels, hidden sugars, and the science of metabolic health.

The initiative has already secured $150 million in seed funding through a coalition of philanthropic organizations, private healthcare networks, and corporate partners. 

While previous high-profile efforts—most notably former First Lady Michelle Obama’s *Let’s Move!* campaign—faced political pushback from agricultural lobbies and school district administrators, Clinton and Gupta insisted their approach would focus on incentives rather than top-down mandates.

“We aren't here to tell people what they can and can’t eat,” Clinton noted. “We are here to level the playing field so that every parent, regardless of their zip code or income, has the ability to nourish their children properly.”

Pilot programs for the Healthy Futures Initiative are set to roll out this fall in ten high-need cities, including Detroit, Atlanta, and Houston, with plans to expand to all 50 states by 2026.

Panelists emphasized that childhood obesity is not simply a matter of personal willpower, but a systemic issue influenced by urban planning, food marketing, and socioeconomic factors. 

"We are living in an environment designed to keep us sedentary," said one panelist. "From suburban layouts that require driving everywhere to screen time replacing outdoor play, we have engineered physical activity out of our daily lives."

### The "Fit Nation" Tour Begins

The New York summit marks the official launch of CNN's broader "Fit Nation" initiative for 2007. Over the coming months, Dr. Gupta and the CNN medical unit will travel to several cities across the country to track community progress, highlight local success stories, and challenge Americans to take control of their health.

"This isn't about running marathons or drastic crash diets," Gupta said. "It's about small, sustainable changes—walking 10,000 steps a day, cutting out soda, eating dinner as a family. If we can get communities to make these changes together, the impact will be enormous."

CNN.com will feature ongoing coverage of the Fit Nation tour, including interactive tools, expert Q&As, user-submitted video diaries, and practical tips for families looking to get fit.
